whats_this.heading: Welcome to Step-Parent Guide
whats_this.description: You're sponsoring or being sponsored by a step-parent. USCIS requires additional documents to confirm that the step-parent relationship qualifies under U.S. immigration law.
quick_instructions: Verify step-parent marriage occurred before age 18.
Checklist all documents you need to gather.
whats_this.disclaimer: Submitting these documents does not automatically guarantee approval. USCIS will review your case and determine whether the step-parent relationship qualifies under U.S. immigration law.

tips: Double-check that names are spelled identically across the child's birth certificate and the marriage certificate. Any discrepancies delay files by months.
Capture the entire sheet including empty margins. USCIS automatically rejects scans where outer boundaries are cut off.
pitfalls: The marriage creating the step-relationship must take place before the child turns 18. This is a strict statutory bar under U.S. immigration law.

tips: Ensure that the child's birth certificate displays the biological parent's full name to establish the chain of connection.
Upload clear and complete scans rather than low-resolution photos.
pitfalls: If either parent was married previously and the termination is not documented, the current marriage is legally void, canceling step-parent status.

tips: Every document not in English must contain both the translation and the signed certification statement to be officially admitted.
pitfalls: Applicants translating their own family certificates leads to automatic RFEs (Request for Evidence) even if perfectly translated.

tips: Make sure names are consistent across all documents. Include legal name change documents if names differ.
pitfalls: Self-translation and unresolved prior marriages are the most frequent reasons for step-parent petition denials.
